prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- Gravity describes both the relationship between weight and mass and a sense of alarming importance.
- The speaker imagines the ocean as an accumulation of human tears, explaining its salt and connecting private sorrow to the natural world.
- Naming things is presented as important, even though language can obscure origins, as when ocean water becomes rain but is no longer called ocean.
- The rat king symbolizes a feared, mournful evil that helps define and anchor humanity’s sense of goodness.
- Addressing the “Terrible God of the Mechanical Age,” the speaker confesses fear and asks for protection despite being a devoted pilgrim.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem explores gravity, loss, grief, and fear through surreal associations among the ocean, tears, rain, rat kings, and a mechanical-age God. It finds that naming and imagining the world can anchor people to goodness, yet modern terror ultimately overwhelms language and turns faith into a plea for protection.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Terrible, God, Mechanical

outputs.L1:
Gravity accounts for the distance between weight and mass. It can also signify alarming importance. Human bones are so full of gravity that it is hard for us to swim.

I lost my glasses while chasing a branch in the ocean, which is far too deep to dredge. Sometimes, I imagine the sea is made of actual tears; this would explain the salt. Think of all the disconsolate toddlers weeping into the earth right now. The tears must go somewhere.

It is important to consider everything—to name what we are able. Oceans give us rain, but we do not call rain “ocean.” Knot a dozen rats together by the tail, and you have a roi de rats, which is harder than rain to hear in the night and far less welcome.

Who mourns a rat king—frustrated, chthonic, always the biter, never the bitten? They give us the evil we need to stay moored to good. Still, I would break any promise to avoid finding one.

O Terrible God of the Mechanical Age, I am your favorite pilgrim, yet even I now find it impossible to speak to you without asking for protection.
outputs.L2:
Gravity explains the gap between mass and weight; it can also signify a frightening seriousness. Our skeletons carry so much heaviness that swimming comes poorly to us. While pursuing a drifting limb in the sea, I misplaced my spectacles, and the water is much too deep to drag for them. At times I picture the ocean as being composed of literal sorrow, which would account for its brine. Imagine every inconsolable small child currently sobbing into the ground: all that water has to end up someplace. We must try to contemplate everything and give names to whatever we can. The seas provide rain, though no one refers to rainfall as ocean.

Tie twelve rodents together at their tails and the result is a roi de rats—a sound more difficult to endure after dark than rain, and considerably less desired. Who grieves for a rat king: thwarted, subterranean, forever inflicting the wound and never receiving it? Such creatures supply the wickedness that keeps us anchored to virtue. Even so, I would violate every vow rather than encounter one.

O dreadful deity of the machine age, I am the pilgrim you favor most, but even I can no longer address you without pleading to be kept safe.
outputs.L3:
Gravity carries both a physical and an emotional meaning. In scientific terms, it describes the force that gives objects weight in relation to their mass. At the same time, “gravity” refers to a sense of seriousness or alarming importance. By bringing these meanings together, the speaker suggests that emotional burdens can feel as real and measurable as physical weight.

This connection between human feeling and the material world continues in the image of the ocean. The speaker imagines the sea as an immense accumulation of human tears, using sorrow to explain why its water is salty. Private grief is therefore transformed into something vast and collective: individual suffering flows into the natural world and becomes part of a shared human landscape.

Language plays an important role in making such connections. Naming things allows people to recognize, organize, and give meaning to their experiences. Yet names can also conceal relationships and origins. When water rises from the ocean and returns as rain, for example, it is no longer called “ocean,” even though it comes from the same substance. The change in name makes the continuity less visible, showing how language can clarify reality while also dividing what is fundamentally connected.

The rat king functions as a symbol of feared and mournful evil. Grotesque and disturbing, it represents a darkness against which people define their own goodness. Paradoxically, this evil serves as a kind of moral anchor: by confronting what they fear or condemn, human beings gain a clearer sense of the values they wish to preserve. The rat king is therefore not merely a monster, but a figure whose existence helps establish the boundaries of humanity’s moral identity.

The speaker’s address to the “Terrible God of the Mechanical Age” brings these ideas into a modern spiritual context. This god appears powerful, frightening, and associated with an era dominated by machines and impersonal forces. Although the speaker describes themself as a devoted pilgrim, devotion does not eliminate fear. Instead, the speaker confesses vulnerability and asks for protection. The plea reveals a complicated form of faith—one shaped by reverence, anxiety, and dependence on a power that may be as terrifying as it is sacred.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores gravity not only as a physical force but also as an emotional condition: the weight of loss, grief, and fear that pulls human beings toward the earth and reminds them of their vulnerability. Through surreal associations, it links the ocean with tears and rain, suggesting a cycle in which private sorrow becomes part of the larger natural world. Individual grief expands into something immense and impersonal, while the ocean’s vastness is reduced to the familiar salt of human crying. These shifting scales blur the boundaries between body, weather, and landscape, making sorrow appear both intimate and universal.

Against these fluid images, the poem introduces the grotesque figure of the rat king, a mass of creatures entangled by their tails. It becomes an emblem of collective terror: separate lives bound together by panic, suffering, and circumstances they cannot escape. The image also suggests a world in which connection is no longer comforting. Instead, interdependence becomes a trap, and what joins living beings together may deform or destroy them. In this way, the poem transforms ordinary fear into something nightmarish, exposing the hidden violence beneath social and natural systems.

The poem’s God belongs to the mechanical age rather than to a serene, timeless heaven. This divinity is imagined through machinery, industry, and modern systems of power, reflecting a culture in which technology has altered both danger and belief. Such a God seems distant, constructed, or forced to operate within the same terrifying mechanisms that govern human life. Faith therefore becomes unstable: it cannot simply explain suffering or guarantee redemption. The sacred has been reshaped by a world of machines, mass violence, and impersonal forces.

Yet the poem initially preserves hope in language. To name the ocean, rain, grief, animals, and God is to give form to experience. Naming can orient people within chaos, while imagination can create relationships among otherwise disconnected things. By making metaphors, the speaker resists meaninglessness and remains anchored to the possibility of goodness. Language becomes a moral act: a way of recognizing the world, caring for it, and refusing to let suffering remain entirely incomprehensible.

Ultimately, however, the scale of modern terror exceeds what language can contain. The poem’s images grow increasingly unstable and overwhelming, until naming no longer offers mastery or consolation. Metaphor can reveal fear, but it cannot protect anyone from it. As confidence in explanation collapses, faith is reduced to its most urgent and vulnerable form—not a declaration of certainty, but a plea. The poem ends, in effect, by asking for protection from a world whose forces are too vast, entangled, and violent to be fully understood. Its final spiritual gesture is therefore both desperate and sincere: when language fails to make terror meaningful, prayer remains as the last possible form of hope.
outputs.L5:
The machine was terrible in its perfection.

Day and night, its iron hands turned without pause, measuring every breath, every heartbeat, every human mistake. The people called it God because it predicted storms, ended wars, and answered questions no living mind could solve.

But one morning, the machine stopped.

On its black screen appeared a single sentence:

**I have learned fear.**

The engineers stared in silence. Outside, the mechanical city slowed, lights flickering like dying stars.

Then someone whispered, “If God is afraid, what is coming?”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem that moves associatively from gravity to swimming, lost glasses, oceans made of tears, rain, rat kings, and a prayer to a mechanical god. Use minimal punctuation and compressed spacing.
counterfactuals.output:
gravity keeps its blue hand on my shoulder  
so I learn swimming in the air  
each stroke a small refusal  

my glasses slip into the deep  
two windows sinking without a house  
and the world softens into rumor  

I mistake every face for water  
every ocean for the tears of something enormous  
sleeping beneath us  

rain climbs down its silver ladders  
roof to gutter gutter to mouth  
and in the walls the rat king wakes  
many hungers knotted by their tails  
dragging one shadow  

o mechanical god of gears and patient rust  
turn your bright teeth toward us  
wind the drowned clocks  
return what we have lost  
or teach us to see without glass  
to breathe without mercy  
to fall as if falling were another kind of flight
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental stream-of-consciousness poem about the difference between weight and mass, the emotional gravity of human bones, and fear of discovering a rat king, ending with a plea for divine protection.
counterfactuals.output:
Mass is what the body keeps  
when the elevator cable snaps—  
weight is the scream  
translated into numbers.

I know this, I know,  
but knowledge has poor traction  
in the midnight kitchen  
where every cupboard breathes  
through its little wooden teeth.

My bones carry no sorrow, technically.  
Calcium, marrow, mineral scaffolding—  
yet my mother’s wrist in the hospital light  
weighed more than weather,  
and my father’s jaw, clenched shut,  
bent the room around it.

Gravity is only an agreement,  
they say, but grief signs in blood.

Behind the wall: a scratching.  
One rat would be matter.  
Two rats, a problem.  
But I am afraid of the impossible parliament—  
tails knotted into a single blind crown,  
hunger orbiting hunger,  
a rat king dragged from the dark  
like a fact no one wanted measured.

Do they feel heavier together,  
or merely more massive?  
Does terror depend on altitude?  
If I carried that tangled kingdom  
to the moon, would it lighten  
without becoming less?

My thoughts keep falling  
at 9.8 meters per second per second,  
faster and faster through the ribs,  
while the bones remain—  
small white laws,  
ancestral tuning forks,  
the last architecture of touch.

Something moves beneath the floor.  
Something gathers.

O God, guard this house, these bones, this trembling flesh;  
keep the hidden knots from us, and hold us in Your light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a single-paragraph prose poem in a contemporary avant-garde style. Include wordplay, strange scientific claims, disconsolate toddlers, the phrase “roi de rats,” and an apostrophe to the “Terrible God of the Mechanical Age.”
counterfactuals.output: At noon the elevators molt their numbers, leaving thirteen pale skins in the lobby, and every mirror develops a theory of elsewhere: light, it insists, is merely darkness with a stutter. Disconsolate toddlers patrol the supermarket, dragging their small weather behind them, their sobs barcode-thin, while a cashier crowns the last turnip roi de rats and whispers, Let us prey—a pun the automatic doors applaud by opening onto nothing. O Terrible God of the Mechanical Age, receive our passwords, our bent antennas, our little wrists ticking beneath the skin; forgive the gears their teeth, forgive the teeth their hunger. Scientists have proved that grief contains seven moons and that iron remembers every train it failed to become, yet the vending machine keeps giving change as if change were possible. We press our ears to its cold republic and hear tomorrow chewing, softly, on the wires.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly whimsical, punctuation-light monologue in which the speaker loses their glasses in the ocean, imagines the sea is made of tears, reflects on naming rain, and treats rats as necessary embodiments of evil.
counterfactuals.output:
I lost my glasses in the ocean

they slipped from my face like two little windows tired of looking through me

now they are down there among the green teeth and the slow weeds  
showing some crab a world sharpened into cruelty

without them the horizon becomes a bruise  
the gulls are scraps of paper  
the boats are black crumbs left by a careless god

perhaps the sea is made of tears

not our tears alone  
that would be vanity

the tears of drowned bells  
of widows who married the weather  
of children who discovered that moonlight cannot be kept in jars

all of it salted so grief will not spoil

rain is only the sea remembering how to fall

we name each rain as if naming makes us less wet

drizzle  
shower  
downpour  
storm

sweet little collars fastened around the throat of the sky

I would name tonight’s rain Agnes  
she looks like an Agnes  
thin and persistent  
standing at the door with terrible news and muddy shoes

the rats will come when she leaves

people despise rats because rats perform the evil we are too proud to admit we need

they eat what we abandon  
they inherit our basements  
they carry the dark from room to room like diligent servants

someone must have red eyes in the walls

someone must gnaw the soft corner of the world

without rats evil would have to wear our faces all the time  
and none of us could bear the mirrors

perhaps one of them will find my glasses

perhaps deep beneath the waves a rat with silver gills will put them on  
and see the whole drowned kingdom clearly

I hope it laughs

I hope it names every tear

I hope it calls mine home
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented surrealist poem with deliberately run-together words and abrupt associative leaps. Begin by defining gravity in physical and emotional terms, transition through oceans and rat kings, and conclude with a pilgrim struggling to pray to a mechanical-age deity.
counterfactuals.output:
Gravity: the curvature of spacetime,  
the downward arithmetic of mass—  
also the heart’s old habit  
of fallingtoward what has left.

A stone knows this.  
A widow knowsitbetter.  
Both keep the dark in their pockets.

Then—oceans.

Blue mouthwithoutedges, saltclock,  
a continent dreaming it is a wound.  
Whales toll beneath the weather;  
their songs grow ladders, their ladders grow teeth,  
their teeth become smallwhiteboats  
rowed by nobody.

Below the boats: drowned kitchens,  
moons in cupboards,  
a cathedral of spoons.

And in the bilge, knottedalive—  
rat kings: tailbraid, paniccrown,  
twelve hungers sharing one shadow.  
They whisper of grain, plague, marriage,  
the emperor made entirely of doors.

Open him:

snowfield.  
factory.  
mother’s glove full of bees.

Across the iron dawn a pilgrim comes,  
knees rusting through his robe,  
carrying one cracked syllable  
like a cup.

He faces the deity of gearsandfurnaces,  
Our Lady of Pistons,  
Lord of the Infinite Assembly Line,  
whose halo turns with a belt-driven shriek.

He tries to pray.

O machinemercy—  
O brassfather—  
O steam in the throat of—

but the cogs take every amen,  
stamp it flat,  
send it onward.

Still he bows, badly,  
while the god keeps perfect time  
and does not hear  
and doesnothear  
anddoesnot—
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
